name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
title: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
answer: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines are the working documents and workflow definitions that let a quantitative analysis be rerun with the same code, data, environment, and results. In this field, a notebook is not just a script with output; it is an executable record that ties narrative, computation, and figures together. A pipeline is the sequence of data preparation, modelling, and reporting steps that can be triggered as a unit. The goal is to remove the gap between what an author saw and what a reader or reviewer can verify.

sections.body: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines are the working documents and workflow definitions that let a quantitative analysis be rerun with the same code, data, environment, and results. In this field, a notebook is not just a script with output; it is an executable record that ties narrative, computation, and figures together. A pipeline is the sequence of data preparation, modelling, and reporting steps that can be triggered as a unit. The goal is to remove the gap between what an author saw and what a reader or reviewer can verify.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on ordinary research workstations, shared compute clusters, and cloud instances, with the environment captured so that it can be recreated. Common building blocks include version control repositories, container images, and package or environment managers. Notebook servers execute code cells in a browser, while pipeline runners schedule steps and pass artifacts between them. Caching layers and artifact stores keep intermediate results so that only changed parts of a workflow need to be recomputed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is to treat an analysis as a sequence of small, inspectable steps rather than a single opaque script. Notebooks are written so that cells run top to bottom and produce the same output on a clean kernel. Pipelines are defined as directed graphs of tasks, with explicit inputs and outputs for each task. Environment pinning, random seeds, and checksums are used to make runs comparable. A finished notebook or pipeline is often executed from scratch in a clean environment as a test of its own reproducibility.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Reproducibility carries rights and risk questions about data access, code licensing, and the provenance of every input and output. A notebook that cannot be rerun because a dependency changed or a dataset was removed creates a silent risk for later work that builds on it. Provenance records, including links to the original papers rather than a search aggregator, help reviewers trace claims back to their sources. The site's library of 135 research papers and 10555 extracted claims reflects this emphasis on traceable evidence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward notebooks and pipelines that are self-contained enough to be moved between machines and institutions without manual setup. More of the environment, including operating system packages and model weights, is being captured in declarative files and containers. Automatic dependency resolution and provenance tracking are becoming part of the workflow rather than an afterthought. The likely result is a tighter link between a published claim and the exact computation that produced it.
